scenes.label: Session 2
scenes.title: Design Thinking
scenes.subtitle: Innovating from real human needs: empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test

beats.say: Welcome to session two. Today we learn Design Thinking: a way to innovate that starts from real human needs, not from technology.

scenes.label: 01 · Why products fail
scenes.title: Iridium: a brilliant idea born from a holiday complaint

cards.title: The spark
cards.text: A Motorola engineer's wife cannot use her mobile phone on holiday in the Caribbean.

cards.title: The vision
cards.text: Effortless communication from and to any corner of the Earth.

cards.title: The product
cards.text: A constellation of satellites giving mobile coverage anywhere on the planet.

beats.say: Let's start with a famous failure. In 1985, the wife of a Motorola engineer complains that she cannot use her mobile phone while on holiday in the Caribbean.
From that complaint comes a huge vision: effortless communication from and to any corner of the Earth.
And a spectacular product: Iridium, a constellation of satellites giving mobile coverage anywhere on the planet. Brilliant engineering. So what went wrong?

scenes.label: The Iridium case
scenes.title: The market had already moved on

stats.label: subscribers Iridium needed to break even
subscribers Iridium actually had in August 1999
GSM mobile subscribers by January 2000, up from 1.3 million in 1994

scenes.banner: Same technology, different users: Iridium found a second life with ships, planes and remote sites with no network at all.

beats.say: Iridium needed about one million subscribers to break even.
In August 1999 it had around twenty thousand.
Meanwhile, ordinary GSM mobile networks had grown from one point three million subscribers in 1994 to four hundred and eighty million by 2000. Most people simply did not need a satellite phone.
Iridium went bankrupt in 1999. Later, it found a second life with the users who really need it: ships, planes and remote sites with no network at all.

scenes.label: Product development
scenes.sub: Everyone loves their own idea. The later you discover a mistake, the more it costs to fix. Ask before you build: who needs this, and how do we know?

beats.say: Engineers call this the cute baby syndrome. Everyone thinks their own baby is beautiful, and every team loves its own idea.
But the later you discover a mistake, the more expensive it is to fix. So ask before you build: who needs this, and how do we know?

scenes.label: 02 · Principles
scenes.title: Three principles behind Design Thinking

cards.title: Empathy
cards.text: Design based on a deep understanding of people.

cards.title: Expansive thinking
cards.text: Go wide before going deep: many options first.

cards.title: Experimentation
cards.text: Build quick prototypes and learn from real reactions.

scenes.banner: P&G put design thinking in its DNA under A.G. Lafley: sales grew from $40B to $83.5B between 2000 and 2008.

beats.say: Design Thinking rests on three principles. Empathy: design from a deep understanding of people.
Expansive thinking: go wide before going deep, and explore many options before choosing one.
And experimentation: build quick prototypes and learn from how people really react.
It is not only for start-ups. Procter and Gamble put customer-centred design into its culture under A.G. Lafley, and its sales grew from forty to over eighty billion dollars in eight years.

steps.title: Define
steps.text: Personas, pain points: frame the right problem.

steps.title: Ideate
steps.text: All ideas are worthy: diverge, then converge.

steps.title: Test
steps.text: What works? Role-play and iterate quickly.

beats.say: The best-known process comes from the Stanford d.school, and it has five steps. Empathize: interview and observe people to understand them.
Define: turn what you learned into a clear problem worth solving.
Ideate: generate many ideas, then converge.
Prototype: make ideas tangible, quickly and cheaply.
And test: put prototypes in front of people, learn, and iterate. Let's go through them one by one.

scenes.label: 03 · Empathize
scenes.title: Ten rules for a great interview

items.title: Ask why
items.text: Even when you think you know.

items.title: Never say “usually”
items.text: Ask for the last specific time.

items.title: Look for inconsistencies
items.text: What people say vs. what they do.

items.title: No binary questions
items.text: Host a conversation, not a survey.

beats.say: Empathy starts with interviews. Talk to a small number of people, five to ten, in depth. Include extreme users: they amplify needs that everyone has. And forget questionnaires: you want stories.

Ask why, even when you think you know. Never ask what people usually do: ask about the last specific time. Encourage stories. Look for inconsistencies between what people say and what they do. And watch their body language.
Embrace silence: it lets people go deeper. Don't suggest answers, and ask neutrally. Avoid yes or no questions. And capture everything: work in pairs, or record.

scenes.label: 04 · Define
scenes.title: Empathy map: says, thinks, does, feels

quads.title: Says
quads.text: Quotes and the exact words they use.

quads.title: Thinks
quads.text: Beliefs and worries they may not say out loud.

scenes.banner: Insights hide in the contradictions, for example between what people say and what they do.

beats.say: Now, define. First organise what you heard in an empathy map, with your user in the centre.
What does the user say? Write their exact words.
What do they think, even if they don't say it?
What do they actually do?
And what do they feel?

Use one sticky note per observation, cluster them, and look for contradictions. That is where the insights are. Personas and customer journey maps help you go further: one gives your user a face and a name, the other shows each step and emotion along the way.

scenes.label: Define
scenes.title: Point of view: frame the right problem

rows.fill: A specific person, not a demographic.
A surprising insight from your research.

scenes.example: A student who studies abroad needs a way to take part in family celebrations, because for her the gift matters less than being part of the moment.

beats.say: Then take a stand with a point of view: one sentence that frames the problem. It has three parts. A specific user. A need, written as a verb, never as a solution. And a surprising insight that explains why.

For example: a student who studies abroad needs a way to take part in family celebrations, because for her the gift matters less than being part of the moment. Different points of view open completely different design spaces.

items.title: Build on the ideas of others

beats.say: Now, ideate. Make ideas visible: doodling and sketching are ways of thinking, and anyone can draw an idea. When you brainstorm as a team, follow seven rules.
Defer judgement. Encourage wild ideas. Build on the ideas of others. Stay on topic.
Hold one conversation at a time. Be visual. And go for quantity: the good ideas usually come after the obvious ones.

scenes.label: 06 · Prototype
scenes.title: Build to think: the prototype is a question

cards.title: Make it tangible
cards.text: A prototype is worth a thousand meetings.

cards.title: Cheap and fast
cards.text: Paper, cardboard, sticky notes before screens.

cards.title: Let them interact
cards.text: Don't explain it: hand it over.

beats.say: If a picture is worth a thousand words, a prototype is worth a thousand meetings. A prototype is a question made tangible.
Keep it cheap and fast: paper, cardboard and sticky notes come before screens.
Don't explain it. Hand it over and let people interact with it.
And fail early, so you can succeed sooner.

scenes.label: 07 · Test
scenes.title: Test to learn: the feedback capture grid
scenes.banner: Show, don't tell. Observe where they hesitate. Capture. Then refine the point of view or the solution, and test again.

beats.say: When you test, show, don't tell. Watch what people do and where they hesitate. And capture the feedback in four boxes.
What did they like?
What would they improve?
What questions did they have?
And which new ideas came up?
Then iterate: refine your point of view or your solution, and test again.

scenes.label: Takeaway
scenes.text: Technology is not the same as need.
scenes.sub:
Empathy is a method. Frame before you solve. Build to learn.
Next session: Business Model Canvas and Lean Startup.

beats.say: To sum up. Iridium had brilliant technology and the wrong users. Technology is not the same as need.

Empathy is a method, not a feeling. Frame the problem before you solve it. And build cheap prototypes to learn, instead of debating. In the next session we will see how to turn a validated need into a business: the Business Model Canvas and Lean Startup.
